findings.title: Plaintext recovery codes are persisted in user storage
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes into a JSON array and passes that as the credential value to user storage via updateCredential. The local path does not do this: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and verifyRecoveryCodeInput (which compares against a hashed saved code) show that local storage keeps only hashes. Recovery codes act as a second factor that bypasses OTP/WebAuthn, so after this change they sit in plaintext in whatever external store backs the user storage (LDAP attribute, external DB). Anyone with read access to that store can obtain usable recovery codes for the user. The codes should be hashed before leaving Keycloak, or the trade-off should be explicitly justified and documented.

findings.title: Exhausted federated recovery-code credential is never removed
findings.body: getCredential now returns credentials from user storage first. When all codes are used, this calls removeStoredCredentialById with the id of that credential. removeStoredCredentialById only operates on the local store (and on user-storage providers that implement UserCredentialStore). For a federated credential the call is a silent no-op, so the spent credential stays in user storage. The CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is still added, but the spent credential is not cleaned up for user-storage-backed users. The test provider does not implement UserCredentialStore and keeps returning the credential. No test covers this path.

findings.title: Undocumented, asymmetric data format for user-storage recovery codes
findings.body: updateCredential receives a JSON array of raw codes (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential). But getCredential passes whatever the provider returns from getCredentials into RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator around line 83 and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean line 19), which expects the local serialized model. The test provider has to convert its stored list via createFromValues inside getCredentials to make this work. Nothing documents this contract for SPI implementers. A provider that returns the stored credential data unchanged, the natural round trip, will likely fail to parse at login or make the login bean throw.

findings.title: Reference provider never consumes recovery codes; single-use is untested
findings.body: The recovery branch of isValid returns true for any stored code and never removes or marks it as used, so this reference provider accepts the same recovery code indefinitely. The new test logs in once with code 0 and never checks that a reused code is rejected or that the next login asks for a different code. Single-use behaviour for user-storage recovery codes is therefore untested, and the provider silently demonstrates the wrong semantics for anyone copying it.

findings.title: Class Javadoc claims this is an unchanged 4.8.3 fixture
findings.body: The Javadoc says this is the Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation and that future versions should work without any change to this provider. This PR adds recovery-code support to the class, a credential type 4.8.3 never had. The comment is now wrong, and the class no longer serves as a frozen 4.8.3 compatibility baseline.

findings.title: Switching to user storage leaves stale local recovery-code credentials
findings.body: When updateCredential succeeds, the local recovery-codes credential is not removed. getCredential then prefers the federated credential, so any previously created local set becomes unreachable for authentication, but it remains in the local store and in stored-credential listings. Regenerating codes after user storage starts supporting the type leaves duplicate, dead recovery credentials.
